frameworks.name: Three Strategic Objectives Filter
frameworks.definition: Every initiative must map to one of three objectives: (1) get more customers, (2) increase LTGP (make customers worth more), or (3) reduce risk that those two things stop happening (increase enterprise value). Anything not mapping to one of these is cut.

frameworks.name: More, Better, New Sequencing
frameworks.definition: Before adding any new initiative, first maximize volume of the best existing activity (More), then optimize its quality and efficiency (Better); only after exhausting both steps should new channels or initiatives be added (New). Most businesses skip straight to New.

frameworks.name: Eight Ways to Get Customers (Core Four + OOP Four)
frameworks.definition: Only four direct acquisition methods exist: warm outreach, cold outreach, paid ads, and content. All four can also be executed by Other People (OOP): customers (referrals), affiliates, employees, and agencies. Every lead strategy maps to one of these eight cells.

frameworks.name: Rule of 100
frameworks.definition: Daily minimum lead-generation activity standard: spend $100 on ads, OR make 100 cold outreaches, OR make 100 warm outreaches, OR produce 100 minutes of content. Volume done consistently at this floor compounds results.

frameworks.name: Impact-Ease Prioritization Matrix
frameworks.definition: Rank all initiatives by two dimensions: impact (revenue or risk effect) and ease (effort required). Execute high-impact/easy tasks first, work down the quadrants, and discard low-impact/hard tasks regardless of how appealing they feel.

frameworks.name: What-Who-How Planning
frameworks.definition: Strategy sessions produce a list of Whats (objectives). Each What must be assigned a Who (person responsible). If the same Who has held the same What for three or more quarters without completing it, the Who is the problem, not the What.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines strategy as prioritizing — specifically, allocating finite resources (time, money, energy) against unlimited options to get the most output per unit of effort. The strategic value of a move is determined by how much it advances the business relative to every other available move, not by how difficult or novel it is.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that every business is constrained by exactly one thing limiting its growth at any moment, and that founders who work maximum hours without growth are working on the wrong constraint — not the real one. Solving the wrong constraint produces zero growth regardless of effort level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business is not growing despite high effort
claims.mechanism: Effort applied to a non-binding constraint produces no growth because the actual bottleneck is unchanged; maximum hours on the wrong activity is indistinguishable from idleness from the business's perspective.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that hopelessness (sadness) in a business context is a signal of ignorance — a lack of perceived options — not a permanent emotional state. When reframed as ignorance, it becomes solvable: acquiring information reveals options and converts hopelessness into a specific, addressable knowledge gap.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Hopelessness is caused by perceived lack of options; options are missing because of ignorance about what is possible; therefore acquiring information about options removes the root cause and eliminates the emotional state.
bounded_by: Anxiety (having options but not knowing which to pick) is a separate signal requiring prioritization, not information

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that anxiety in a business context is a signal of unclear priority — having too many options without a framework for choosing among them. Anxiety is resolved not by gathering more information but by developing a prioritization criterion (strategy).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Anxiety originates from unresolved choice among many options; adding information worsens it; only a prioritization criterion resolves the decision-paralysis causing the anxiety.
bounded_by: Hopelessness (no options at all) requires information-gathering, not prioritization

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that cutting the unprofitable 85% of a customer base and refocusing entirely on the profitable 15% — combined with avatar-specific messaging and a 10x price increase — produced 10x company growth in a PR agency portfolio company, selling more units at higher prices than the original mixed-avatar model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Recurring-service business where a small minority of customers account for disproportionate LTV
Willingness to accept nine-month revenue trough during transition
claims.mechanism: Removing low-value customers forces niche-specific messaging precision, which raises conversion among the high-value segment; simultaneously the 10x price increase selects for buyers who value the service, reducing churn and increasing LTGP.

anchors.value: 15% of customers, paid most and stayed longest

bounded_by: Required nine-month near-zero revenue period before recovery; not viable for businesses with no cash runway

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that output equals volume multiplied by leverage, meaning a founder who is unwilling to work high volumes must compensate with disproportionately high leverage per action to achieve the same business output. There is no shortcut that bypasses both volume and leverage simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that for a business run by a solo owner whose death would end the business, transitioning from $2M to $3M annual income adds roughly $10 million to net worth (at approximately 10x EBITDA multiple), whereas the same $1M income increase in a business that does not depend on the owner adds a multiple of that in enterprise value — making net worth growth from asset building far exceed income optimization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business generates $2M annual profit
Business is valued at 10-15x earnings multiple (varies by industry)
claims.mechanism: A founder-independent business can be operated by a new owner without retraining, which adds a transferability premium; each incremental dollar of profit in a transferable business is multiplied by the earnings multiple to produce net worth, whereas the same dollar in a founder-dependent business produces only face value.

numbers.axis: incremental net worth per $1M income increase

anchors.value: higher multiple, compounding net worth advantage

bounded_by: Multiple varies significantly by industry (10x, 15x, 20x cited as range)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the primary difference between small businesses and large businesses is the number of A-players employed, not strategy, market, or product quality. Large business owners maintain a lower tolerance for mediocrity — they keep searching until they fill all critical roles with high performers rather than accepting the first adequate hire.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that a mediocre team member who is consuming founder attention and causing concern occupies approximately 25% of the founder's mental bandwidth — representing an enormous hidden cost that directly limits strategic thinking and growth-oriented work.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The person is creating concern but not contributing net positive value

numbers.axis: founder bandwidth consumed by problem employee

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that the biggest single growth lever for most founders is on the other side of a few hard conversations with underperforming team members — implying the decision not to have those conversations is functionally equivalent to choosing poverty, not avoiding discomfort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has identified a team member who is clearly underperforming but has not addressed it
claims.mechanism: Retaining underperformers blocks the slot that an A-player would fill, prevents the performance improvement or exit that would unlock growth, and consumes disproportionate management bandwidth — compounding the growth deficit.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that when a team member is given the same task quarter after quarter and does not complete it, the Who (person) is the problem, not the What (task). Winners on a team execute immediately, take things off the founder's plate, and create momentum; this pattern of execution is the observable definition of talent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Same task assigned for 12+ weeks with no completion

anchors.value: same task for 3+ consecutive quarters (12+ weeks)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most small business owners default to pursuing New initiatives before exhausting More (volume) and Better (quality/efficiency) improvements on their existing highest-leverage activity — and this pattern of premature new-channel expansion is the primary growth killer in small businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: New channels have unknown conversion rates and require new learning curves; existing channels have proven paths, known metrics, and trained teams — so doubling a working channel almost always has higher expected value than launching an unproven one.
bounded_by: Only applies after More and Better have been genuinely exhausted on the current best channel

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Gym Launch grew from approximately $3M/year to $37M/year not because of new strategies but because Layla Hormozi built a team that systematically executed the existing strategy at increasing volume and quality — and the business grew 40% more after Hormozi exited the majority share because the new CEO Cale focused exclusively on More and Better rather than New.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Established business with proven core acquisition and delivery model
claims.mechanism: Systematically executing known winning activities at higher volume and with incremental quality improvements compounds nonlinearly over time, producing revenue growth without the risk or learning curve of new channels.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the $100M Offers book sold 25,000 copies per month (approximately 1,000 copies per day) with zero marketing spend at the time of this talk, driven entirely by word of mouth — the result of two years invested in making the product exceptional rather than two months followed by constant promotion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Book priced at $0.99 at launch
Initial platform: ~20,000 Instagram followers only
claims.mechanism: An exceptional product generates referrals at a rate that grows nonlinearly (two bring four, four bring eight); the compounding referral loop replaces paid acquisition entirely once the product quality threshold is crossed. A mediocre product marketed heavily only accelerates proof of mediocrity.
bounded_by: Required two years of writing investment and initial willingness to price at $0.99

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that businesses with the highest LTV (lifetime gross profit) can spend the most on customer acquisition and therefore outcompete on marketing — not because they are better at marketing tactics, but because their backend economics allow them to operate at acquisition costs that competitors cannot sustain.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Competitive paid acquisition environment
claims.mechanism: Marketing spend is limited by the maximum CAC a business can absorb while remaining profitable; a business with 3x LTV can pay 3x CAC and still win, crowding out competitors with lower LTV regardless of their marketing sophistication.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines learning — operationally — as producing a new behavior under the same stimulus condition. Rate of learning equals the speed at which behavior changes when conditions remain constant. By this definition, attending an event without changing behavior afterward means zero learning has occurred, regardless of how much information was absorbed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not distinguish understanding from execution; a person who understands but does not act is classified as not having learned by this definition

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that wealth is built through asset ownership, not income optimization — and that many founders spend disproportionate time on tax minimization of income while neglecting to grow the enterprise value of the asset that will actually determine their net worth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder with a business generating meaningful profit
claims.mechanism: Income is consumed or invested externally at market rates of return; enterprise value of a growing business compounds at rates that exceed passive investment and is realized as a lump sum at exit, making it the dominant driver of founder net worth.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that referrals are nonlinear (exponential) in nature — two bring four, four bring eight — making them the highest-leverage growth vehicle available, but only accessible to businesses whose product quality crosses the threshold at which customers voluntarily refer others.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product or service quality is genuinely high enough that satisfied customers proactively recommend it
claims.mechanism: Each satisfied customer who refers generates their own pool of potential referrers, creating compounding growth that does not require proportional marketing spend; below the quality threshold, referrals do not activate and the mechanism does not operate.
bounded_by: Only activates when product quality is high enough to generate unsolicited referrals — cannot be manufactured with marketing for a mediocre product

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a franchise or multi-unit business's profitability per unit is the foundational constraint on scalability — and that attempting to scale marketing or franchise sales before fixing per-unit margins is structurally futile regardless of brand awareness or acquisition skill.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Franchise or multi-unit brick-and-mortar business
Per-unit margins are insufficient to justify capital deployment
claims.mechanism: Poor per-unit economics multiply linearly with scale — each new unit adds the same margin drag; marketing or franchise sales growth cannot compensate for structurally broken unit economics and only speeds capital destruction.
bounded_by: A business with strong per-unit margins benefits from marketing investment; this claim applies specifically where the unit economics are the primary defect

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes a franchise client whose 20-location chain had top-line revenue of approximately $1.3M per location with less than $150K profit (below ~12% net margin) and whose 10 years of attempted scaling had produced no improvement — diagnosing the root cause as operational complexity (500-item menu) and poor vendor economics, not marketing deficiency.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Franchise model, ~20 locations (6 corporate, 14 franchised)
~$1M per location opening cost

claims.text: Alex Hormozi proposes that a 1%-per-month incremental margin recovery plan — identifying and recovering 1 percentage point of profit each month for 12 consecutive months — is sufficient to transform a structurally broken franchise from unsellable to investable and to triple net margin within one year.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Franchise or multi-unit business with identified operational inefficiencies
Margin currently 10-15% with known improvement levers (menu simplification, vendor renegotiation)
claims.mechanism: Each 1% margin recovery is compounding: it increases total profit, which raises valuation multiple, which improves franchisee economics and the investability of the model. Twelve sequential 1% recoveries triple a 10% base margin to 22%+.
bounded_by: Requires operational discipline to execute one improvement per month without distraction from marketing or expansion

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes a YouTube channel with 40M+ subscribers that approached Acquisition.com wanting to improve their media production system — which was already at a ~97/100 quality level — while monetizing exclusively through AdSense. Hormozi diagnosed that the binding constraint was not production quality but the absence of any product to sell; moving from zero to a 20/100 product offering would generate 10x more revenue than optimizing production from 97 to 99. The channel was working on a non-binding constraint while the actual constraint (nothing to sell) remained unsolved.

Alex Hormozi describes a PR company in the Acquisition.com portfolio where 85% of customers churned within 2-3 months and 15% paid the most and stayed the longest. He advised the founder to stop selling to the 85% entirely, rebuild messaging for the 15% avatar specifically, and 10x the price. After a nine-month near-zero revenue transition — during which Hormozi spoke with the founder weekly to maintain conviction — the business closed more units than before at 10x the previous price, achieving 10x company value. The example illustrates how cutting volume in favor of quality can produce orders-of-magnitude better outcomes than trying to grow the mixed-avatar model.

Alex Hormozi describes a dentist association where 500 dentists pooled buying power, saved $30K/year each, and paid the association $10K/year — a strong sticky model the founder believed worth $20-30M at exit. Hormozi reframed the strategy: bundle 10 dentist practices per year into roll-up packages selling at $100M each (20% retained, 80% to dentists), generating $20-30M/year in profit from the roll-up machine itself. At a 10x earnings multiple, that machine would be worth $200-300M versus the $25M direct exit — an example of a strategic move that takes the entrepreneur entirely off the original game board.

Alex Hormozi describes his GMAT preparation as a clean input-output example: research showed that number of practice problems solved correlated directly with test score. He solved four hours of problems per day for 16 weeks — accumulating a phone-book-height stack — and ultimately scored above Harvard median. By the time he sat the actual test, he had seen and solved every problem type at least 100 times. The example illustrates that identifying a clean input-output equation and then doing massive volume on that input is sufficient to achieve exceptional results.

Alex Hormozi describes Gym Launch's growth from approximately $3M to $37M annual revenue as driven primarily by Layla Hormozi building a team structure that empowered employees and removed tasks from Alex's calendar — not new strategies. After Alex and Layla exited their majority share in 2021, new CEO Cale grew the business an additional 40% by refusing new initiatives (e.g., declining TikTok) in favor of doubling the cold call team and improving scripts and personalization. No single new thing drove the 40% growth; it was many small improvements compounded.

Alex Hormozi describes his $100M Offers book as an example of two-year product investment yielding compounding returns: he spent a long time writing it, launched at $0.99, made a single post to approximately 20,000 Instagram followers, and generated no paid advertising. At the time of this talk, the book sells approximately 25,000 copies per month (roughly 1,000 per day), increasing month over month, with 14,000 five-star reviews — all from word of mouth. He contrasts this with a hypothetical two-month mediocre book requiring lifetime paid promotion: that path requires constant marketing spend that never ends, whereas the exceptional product markets itself.

Alex Hormozi describes a franchise client with approximately 20 locations (6 corporate, 14 franchised), ~$1M opening cost per unit, ~$1.3M top-line and <$150K profit per location, who had spent 10 years trying to improve franchise marketing. Hormozi diagnosed that the constraint was operational: a 500-item menu driving high COGS, bad vendor deals, and thin margins. He proposed ignoring marketing entirely for 12 months and instead recovering 1% net margin per month through menu simplification to 15 items and vendor renegotiation. After 12 months, the business would be sellable, investable, and at triple or more the original net profit.

practices.text: Write down the name of any team member whose performance you know is inadequate and initiate a 14-day Performance Improvement Plan: state the specific behaviors that must change within 14 days or the person exits.
When managing a team, say directly to the person's face what you currently say about them behind their back. Do not soften, qualify, or defer the conversation.
When evaluating any proposed initiative, ask: does this get us more customers, make customers worth more, or reduce the risk that the first two stop happening? If it maps to none of these, cut it.

Before opening new acquisition channels, ask whether the existing best channel can be doubled in volume first (More), then whether conversion, speed, or personalization can be improved without new resources (Better). Only after both are exhausted should a new channel be added (New).
Apply the Rule of 100 daily for lead generation: $100 in ad spend, OR 100 cold outreaches, OR 100 warm outreaches, OR 100 minutes of content — pick one and do it every day without exception.
When evaluating a business constraint, ask: why can't we 10x this business? The answer usually immediately reveals the actual binding constraint.

Before investing in marketing, verify that churn is low enough to justify acquisition spend: if the business would not survive three to four months without selling any new customers, fix the back end first.

When building toward multi-location or franchise scale, strip the model to its simplest operational form — minimum square footage, minimum SKUs or services, minimum headcount — before replicating. Simplicity is what makes the unit economics scalable.
